name: Bianca Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking to me, Bianca. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent: no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and we're not selling anything. It's all confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say out loud and what you really think. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at the Highridge Electric depot at half six, up in the mountains, and the first thing I do is walk round the digger-derrick truck, the one with the auger for drilling pole holes and the boom for lifting poles. I drive it because I drove trucks for 25 years and nobody else on the crew can back it down a forest track like I can. Then it's whatever's broken: snow load snapping a line, a pole hit by a car on the pass road, old wire that needs restringing. I'm an apprentice, so once we're there, I'm learning, and I'm slower than the kids at the climbing and the knots.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Why the move from trucking at 55?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My back was tired of sitting, and I was tired of motel rooms. My husband Karl has his own electrical firm, house wiring mostly, and he said if you want to be home every night, the power company pays well and you already know heavy vehicles. We've paid off the house and we've got a small cabin by the lake we rent out in summer, so I wasn't doing it for the money exactly. I just didn't want to retire yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I've heard this one before. For fifteen years they told us self-driving trucks would take my old job, and I drove right up to the day I quit. At work I'd laugh about it with Arturo, the journeyman I eat lunch with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means nothing changes. I learn the trade, I keep driving the derrick truck, and I work till 64 or so. Karl's firm keeps going, the cabin keeps renting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bianca keeps going with her apprenticeship and her driving. She'd keep using the AI chatbot now and then, the way she does to plan the cabin's booking messages, and keep her money where it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit smug, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You say you use a chatbot for the cabin bookings. What else do you use it for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly writing. I'm not good at nice emails, so I get it to make my messages to guests sound friendly. My daughter Nina showed me. I tried asking it about rigging once and it said something I knew was wrong, so I stick to emails.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Karl if this turned out to be the case?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say keep your van, keep your tools, the houses still need wiring. He's been worried about some of those smart home things changing his work. In this picture, he'd be fine.

S0.say: I'd say I've heard this before, since they spent fifteen years saying self-driving trucks would take my old job. I'd laugh about it at lunch with Arturo.
S0.think: Privately nothing changes: she learns the trade, keeps driving the derrick truck and works till about 64. Karl's firm and the cabin rental carry on.
S0.do: Keeps going with her apprenticeship and driving. Keeps using the chatbot now and then for cabin booking messages and leaves her money where it is.
S0.quote: I tried asking it about rigging once and it said something I knew was wrong, so I stick to emails.
S0.fieldNote: Bianca's scepticism comes from years of hearing that self-driving trucks would replace her. She uses AI in a narrow, practical way and has already found its limits on technical questions. Her concern for her husband's electrical firm appears early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's like any new equipment: some of it works, some doesn't, and you find out on the job. At the depot I'd say let's try it before we panic. I'm not one for posting online, maybe a comment on the trucking forum I still read.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think line work will change a bit and Karl's firm might change more. The drones and sensors would help us find faults on the pass faster, which I'd like. If smart wiring gets easier, Karl might lose some of the small jobs that pay his bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bianca would take the company training on any new fault-finding system once the crew had used it for a few months. She'd sit down with Karl and look at whether his firm should take on an apprentice who knows the new smart systems. She'd keep putting cabin rent into savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit of worry for Karl in the back of my mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If Highridge brought in drones for the line patrols, how would that change your day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Less driving up forest tracks in the dark to look at a line, which honestly I'd miss a bit. But in a snowstorm, if a drone tells us exactly which span is down, that's two hours saved and nobody sliding off the road. I'd take that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Karl might lose small jobs. What would you tell him?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That he's 61 and doesn't need to chase every job. He could wind down the small stuff and keep the big renovations. We've got enough, it's more about him feeling useful.

S1.say: I'd say it's like any new equipment: some works, some doesn't, and you find out on the job. At the depot I'd say let's try it before we panic.
S1.think: Privately she thinks line work changes a bit and Karl's firm might change more. Drones would help find faults faster, but easier smart wiring could take Karl's small jobs.
S1.do: Takes company training on new fault-finding systems once the crew has used them for a few months. Sits down with Karl to consider an apprentice skilled in smart systems and keeps saving the cabin rent.
S1.feel: Mostly calm, with background worry for Karl.
S1.quote: If a drone tells us exactly which span is down, that's two hours saved and nobody sliding off the road.
S1.fieldNote: She's steady and practical, ready to adopt tools once proven by the crew. Her thinking keeps returning to Karl's business rather than her own job. She'd miss the night drives but values the safety gain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is going too fast for anyone to handle well, companies or government. At the depot I'd say we need to hear from management what the plan is. I wouldn't be shouting, but I'd be asking hard questions at the safety meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be thinking about Karl first. If robots can wire houses in two years, his firm's done, and he's 63 then, with two lads working for him. My own job I'd lose too, but I'd be 60 and fine with the money. His firm is his whole sense of himself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bianca would retire at 60 once robots were clearly working on Highridge lines. She'd help Karl plan how to close his firm well, giving his two workers notice and helping them find something. She'd keep the cabin rented and hold off on the new kitchen they'd planned for next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not for me, for Karl and his lads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years' notice, what does the short time change for you both?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No time to wind down properly. With two years, Karl would be closing a firm in a rush, and his lads would be looking for work along with everyone else. If we had longer, he could sell it or hand it on, but two years means just shutting the door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Karl's two workers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them what I know about trucking: learn the bit the robot can't do yet, and get ahead of the others. Dmitri's 29, he'll find something. The older one, Pat, he's 52, and he worries me.

S2.say: I'd say this is going too fast for companies or government to handle well. At the depot safety meeting I'd ask hard questions about management's plan.
S2.think: Privately she thinks first of Karl, whose wiring firm could be done in two years when he's 63. She'd lose her own job too, but at 60 she's fine for money; his firm is his sense of himself.
S2.do: Retires at 60 once robots are working on Highridge lines and helps Karl close his firm well, giving his two workers notice and helping them look for work. Keeps the cabin rented and holds off on the planned new kitchen.
S2.feel: Anxious, mainly for Karl and his workers.
S2.quote: If we had longer, he could sell it or hand it on, but two years means just shutting the door.
S2.fieldNote: Bianca's anxiety is about her husband's business and his workers, not her own finances. The short warning time matters because it takes away the chance to sell or hand on the firm. She blames speed, not any one villain, in keeping with her centre outlook.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is tight but workable. At the depot I'd say let's see the plan and get people trained. I'd tell friends who run small businesses to start thinking about selling while they can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years means Karl can sell the firm while it's still worth something. I'd get my card, work three years or so, and stop at 63. It's still fast, but there's room to do it decently.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bianca would finish her apprenticeship, then keep driving and working until about 63. She'd help Karl find a buyer for the firm in the next two or three years, while it's still worth something. She'd keep saving the cabin rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in control. We'd have time to do it properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn the new robot systems in that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Highridge asked me, yes, once Arturo had tried them. I'd probably end up as the one who drives the robot out on the truck and sets it up. That's not a bad job for an old trucker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the hardest part of five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Watching it coming. With two years you just react. With five, you see it every day and you have to decide when to go, and that's harder for some people than just being told.

S3.say: I'd say five years is tight but workable. I'd tell friends with small businesses to start thinking about selling while they can.
S3.think: Privately five years means Karl can sell his firm while it's still worth something. She'd get her card, work a few years and stop at 63.
S3.do: Finishes her apprenticeship and keeps driving and working until about 63. Helps Karl find a buyer for the firm in the next two or three years and keeps saving the cabin rent.
S3.feel: Uneasy but in control, with time to do it properly.
S3.quote: That's not a bad job for an old trucker.
S3.fieldNote: With five years the household's main move is selling Karl's firm while it has value. Bianca sees herself driving robots to the job and setting them up, a practical fit with her trucking past. Her observation that seeing it coming can be harder than reacting is thoughtful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty if people are sensible. At the depot I'd say let's not lose sleep over it yet. I'd mostly say it to Karl, and tell him to plan his exit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, this one hardly touches us. Karl would retire around 66 anyway, and I'd stop at 64. By 2036 we're both done and watching from the cabin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bianca keeps going with her plan: apprenticeship, card, retire around 64. She'd encourage Karl to train up Dmitri to take over the firm over the decade, and keep the cabin as their retirement project.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's a long way off for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes most for you between two years and ten?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Karl's firm. With two years, he shuts the door. With ten, he hands the keys to Dmitri and walks away proud. That's worth a lot to him, and so to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell your children anything different with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Nina and Paul to look hard at their jobs now. Nina's in insurance and Paul drives a delivery van, of all things. Ten years is a long time to get ready, but only if they start.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty if people are sensible, and there's no need to lose sleep yet. Mostly I'd tell Karl to plan his exit.
S4.think: Privately it hardly touches them: Karl would retire around 66 and she'd stop at 64. By 2036 they're both finished and watching from the cabin.
S4.do: Keeps going with her plan to qualify and retire around 64. Encourages Karl to train his young worker to take over the firm over the decade and keeps the cabin as their retirement project.
S4.feel: Calm, since it's a long way off for them.
S4.quote: With ten, he hands the keys to Dmitri and walks away proud.
S4.fieldNote: For Bianca the warning time is measured in what it does to her husband's business, from shutting the door to handing on the keys. Her own job barely registers. She'd push her grown children to look at their jobs now.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because Karl's firm would just close and his lads would be out on the street with everyone else. What would help is time, really, or something to stand in for time: help for small firms to wind down or sell, and money for people like Pat to retrain.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what people like me know that a robot doesn't. I know which forest tracks wash out in spring and which bends on the pass ice over first. Somebody should write that down before all of us retire.

headlineQuote: I know which forest tracks wash out in spring and which bends on the pass ice over first.
portrait: Bianca Weber drove trucks for 25 years before joining Highridge Electric as an apprentice at 55, where she drives the digger-derrick truck on mountain roads. She's steady and practical, uses AI for friendly emails to cabin guests, and is sceptical after years of empty self-driving truck predictions. With a paid-off house and a rented lake cabin, her own finances aren't at risk, so her worry centres on her husband Karl's electrical firm and his two workers. The amount of warning decides whether Karl shuts his door in a rush or hands the firm on with pride.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because her husband's firm would close in a rush and his workers would lose their jobs along with everyone else.
whatWouldHelp: Help for small firms to wind down or sell, and money for older workers like Pat to retrain.
